Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Temporomandibular disorders (TMD)

Reviews of randomized trials report average reductions in pain and gains in mouth opening, while individual trials show outcome-specific results, including pain and function improvement without a clear change in jaw range of motion.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Reviews of randomized trials report average reductions in pain and gains in mouth opening, while individual trials show outcome-specific results, including pain and function improvement without a clear change in jaw range of motion.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Oral > TMD category contains 159 titles: 108 human clinical publications, 12 animal studies, 28 systematic reviews, meta-analyses, or reviews, nine protocols, one in-vitro study, and one unclassified record. Review counts overlap because several papers synthesize the same trials; the 108 human publications are not 108 independent cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2025 systematic review analyzed 44 randomized trials with 1,816 participants and reported average reductions in pain and improvements in maximum mouth opening, while also noting variation in laser parameters and treatment schedules (Díaz et al. 2025). In one sham-controlled double-blind trial, 30 women received six sessions of intraoral PBM or sham. Pain and functional scale scores favored PBM, but mandibular range of motion did not differ significantly (Herpich et al. 2020). The clinical findings therefore depend on which outcome and TMD presentation are examined.

Animal evidence

Twelve animal studies are listed, eight in rats and four in rabbits. They test joint or muscle pain models and cannot establish patient symptom relief.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One standalone in-vitro study is listed. No separate ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The review describes commonly studied wavelengths from 810 to 940 nm and fluences around 3–12 J/cm². The clinical record also includes intraoral combinations such as 905-nm super-pulsed laser with 640-nm red and 875-nm near-infrared LEDs. Routes, treatment points, schedules, diagnostic subtypes, and outcomes vary, limiting direct protocol comparisons.

Interpretation

The evidence supports short-term pain and jaw-opening improvement in some TMD groups, but it does not establish a uniform or durable effect across muscular and joint disorders.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term pain and jaw-opening improvement in selected TMD populations Low for durable benefit across TMD subtypes and outcomes
Publications and records159 unique titles in the exact TMD category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The literature includes many randomized trials, but reviews reuse the same underlying studies and protocols vary by diagnosis, route, device, and dose. A recent review found average pain and mouth-opening gains, while sham-controlled trials show that benefits can differ by outcome. Longer follow-up and subtype-specific trials would strengthen conclusions.
